questions.question: What is Spring Boot and how is it different from the Spring Framework?
questions.title: What is Spring Boot vs Spring Framework
questions.direct_answer: Spring Framework is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications — but it requires extensive XML or Java configuration for every feature. Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of Spring that eliminates boilerplate: it auto-configures components, embeds a web server (Tomcat), and lets you start coding business logic immediately with minimal setup. Think of Spring as a fully customizable toolkit, and Spring Boot as a pre-assembled workstation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that Spring Boot isn't a separate framework but a convenience layer — and whether you've actually built something with it or just read about it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Spring Boot replaces Spring — it doesn't. It uses Spring under the hood and just reduces configuration pain.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain auto-configuration: Spring Boot reads your classpath (do you have spring-boot-starter-web? Then it auto-configures Tomcat, Jackson, DispatcherServlet). Mention starter POMs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Boot IS Spring** — it's not a replacement; it auto-configures the same Spring beans you'd configure manually
- **Auto-configuration reads the classpath** — add `spring-boot-starter-web` and Tomcat, Jackson, and DispatcherServlet are configured automatically
- **Starter dependencies bundle compatible libraries** — one dependency like `starter-web` replaces 15 individual library declarations with tested versions
- **Embedded server = executable JAR** — `java -jar app.jar` starts Tomcat inside; no external server installation, ideal for Docker/Kubernetes
- **`@SpringBootApplication` = three annotations** — combines `@Configuration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan` in one

Imagine you want to build a house. The Spring Framework gives you every possible tool, material, and blueprint — but you have to assemble everything yourself. You choose the foundation, wire the electricity, plumb the pipes, one piece at a time. You have ultimate control, but setup takes days before you can even hang a picture.

Spring Boot hands you a move-in-ready house. The plumbing works, the electricity is on, and you have a key. You can immediately start decorating — which is what matters (your business logic). If you don't like the default light fixtures, you can still swap them out.

Technically, Spring Boot does three major things:

**1. Auto-Configuration** — When you add `spring-boot-starter-web` to your dependencies, Spring Boot sees Tomcat and Spring MVC on the classpath and automatically configures an embedded web server, a JSON serializer (Jackson), and a request dispatcher. You didn't write a single line of configuration.

**2. Starter Dependencies** — Instead of manually adding 15 individual libraries for web development (servlet API, Tomcat, Jackson, validation, etc.), you add one dependency: `spring-boot-starter-web`. It pulls everything you need in compatible versions.

**3. Embedded Server** — Traditional Spring apps produce a WAR file you deploy to an external Tomcat. Spring Boot apps produce a JAR with Tomcat embedded inside. You run `java -jar app.jar` and your server starts. This is crucial for containerized deployments (Docker, Kubernetes).

## What Spring Boot Automates and How

Spring Boot's magic is not magic — it's a set of well-defined conventions that eliminate repetitive configuration. Understanding the mechanism makes you faster at debugging when auto-configuration does something unexpected.

### Auto-Configuration: Reading the Classpath

When your application starts, Spring Boot scans every JAR on your classpath for `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`. Each listed class is a `@Configuration` that conditionally creates beans.

The key annotation is `@ConditionalOnClass` — it says "only activate this configuration if a specific class exists on the classpath." For example:

```java
// From Spring Boot internals (simplified)
@Configuration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)         // only if JDBC is on classpath
@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "spring.datasource.url")  // only if URL is configured
public class DataSourceAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                 // only if user hasn't defined their own
    public DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create()
            .url(props.getUrl())
            .username(props.getUsername())
            .build();
    }
}
```

The `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is critical: if you define your own `DataSource` bean, auto-configuration backs off. You always have the final say. This is the "opinionated but not dictatorial" philosophy.

### Starter Dependencies: Curated Library Sets

A starter is a Maven POM (or Gradle module) that pulls in a group of compatible libraries. `spring-boot-starter-web` brings:
- Spring MVC (web framework)
- Embedded Tomcat (web server)
- Jackson (JSON serialization)
- Hibernate Validator (request validation)
- SLF4J + Logback (logging)

Without starters, you'd manually add each library and hope the versions are compatible. Starters guarantee version compatibility through Spring Boot's dependency management BOM (Bill of Materials).

```xml
<!-- ONE dependency replaces 10+ individual library declarations -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <!-- version managed by parent POM — no version tag needed -->
</dependency>
```

### Embedded Server: JAR vs WAR Deployment

Traditional Java web applications produce a **WAR** file that you deploy to an external Tomcat server. This means installing, configuring, and maintaining Tomcat separately — and deploying means copying a WAR into Tomcat's `webapps/` folder.

Spring Boot embeds Tomcat (or Jetty, or Undertow) inside your JAR. The result: `java -jar myapp.jar` starts your entire application. No external server installation, no WAR deployment, no Tomcat configuration files.

```bash
# Traditional (WAR)
# 1. Install Tomcat
# 2. Configure server.xml, context.xml
# 3. Build WAR: mvn package
# 4. Copy target/myapp.war to /opt/tomcat/webapps/
# 5. Start Tomcat: /opt/tomcat/bin/startup.sh

# Spring Boot (JAR)
mvn package                      # builds executable JAR with embedded Tomcat
java -jar target/myapp-1.0.jar   # done — server starts inside the JAR
```

This is essential for **containerized deployments** (Docker, Kubernetes). A Docker image just needs a JRE and your JAR — no Tomcat layer to maintain:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY target/myapp-1.0.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

### application.properties vs application.yml

Spring Boot reads configuration from `application.properties` (or `application.yml`) in `src/main/resources/`. Every auto-configured bean reads its settings from here:

```properties
# Server
server.port=8080
server.servlet.context-path=/api

# Database
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb
spring.datasource.username=admin
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}  # environment variable

# JPA
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true

# Profiles — environment-specific config
# application-dev.properties  (activate: --spring.profiles.active=dev)
# application-prod.properties (activate: --spring.profiles.active=prod)
```

**Profiles** let you maintain separate configs per environment. `application-dev.properties` might use H2 in-memory database while `application-prod.properties` uses PostgreSQL. Activate with `--spring.profiles.active=prod` at startup.

### Spring Boot Actuator: Production Monitoring

Adding `spring-boot-starter-actuator` exposes HTTP endpoints for health checks, metrics, and environment info:

```
GET /actuator/health    → {"status": "UP"}
GET /actuator/metrics   → JVM memory, thread counts, HTTP request stats
GET /actuator/env       → all configuration properties (sanitized)
GET /actuator/info      → build version, git commit, custom metadata
```

Kubernetes uses `/actuator/health` for liveness and readiness probes. Prometheus scrapes `/actuator/prometheus` for metrics. These endpoints are what make Spring Boot applications production-ready out of the box.

- Spring Boot IS Spring — it's not a replacement. Under the hood, it configures the same Spring beans you would configure manually.
- @SpringBootApplication is three annotations in one: @Configuration (this class has bean definitions), @EnableAutoConfiguration (let Spring Boot configure things), @ComponentScan (find my @Controller, @Service, @Repository classes)
- application.properties (or .yml) replaces most XML config — server.port=8080, spring.datasource.url, etc.
- Spring Boot DevTools gives auto-restart on code changes during development — saves the compile-deploy cycle
- The Spring Initializr (start.spring.io) generates a project skeleton with your chosen starters in seconds
Create a minimal Spring Boot application with a /api/health endpoint that returns {"status": "UP"}. Use only @SpringBootApplication and @RestController. Run it and test with curl or a browser.

questions.question: What is Dependency Injection in Spring and why does it matter?
questions.title: Dependency Injection in Spring Explained
questions.direct_answer: Dependency Injection (DI) means a class doesn't create its own dependencies — they're provided (injected) from outside. Instead of UserService creating its own UserRepository with `new UserRepository()`, Spring creates the UserRepository and passes it into UserService. This makes code testable (you can inject a mock), loosely coupled (swapping implementations doesn't change UserService), and easier to maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you explain DI without jargon? Do you understand WHY it matters for real projects — testability, maintainability — not just what it is?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing DI with the @Autowired annotation — DI is a design principle, @Autowired is just Spring's way of doing it. Also mixing up IoC and DI.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the 'before and after' — code without DI (tightly coupled, hard to test) vs code with DI (clean, testable). Mention constructor injection as the preferred approach.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DI means classes don't create their own dependencies** — the IoC container creates objects and wires them together automatically
- **Constructor injection is preferred** — makes dependencies explicit, supports `final` fields for immutability, and works in tests without Spring
- **Interface-based design enables swapping** — inject `UserRepository` (interface), not `JpaUserRepository` (implementation); change backends without touching service code
- **Testing is trivial with DI** — inject a mock `UserRepository` in tests; no real database needed, tests run in milliseconds
- **`@Qualifier` resolves ambiguity** — when multiple beans implement the same interface, `@Qualifier("beanName")` tells Spring which one to inject

Think of it like ordering food. Without DI, you go to the kitchen, buy ingredients, cook the meal yourself — your code creates its own dependencies. With DI, a waiter brings you the food — someone else prepared it, and you just consume it.

Here's why this matters in real code:

**Without DI (tightly coupled):**
Without DI, imagine `UserService` constructing `new MySQLUserRepository()` right inside the class—that implementation is baked in.
Problems: (1) You can't test UserService without a real MySQL database. (2) Switching to PostgreSQL means changing UserService code. (3) UserService knows too much about its dependencies.

**With DI (loosely coupled):**
With DI, `UserService` holds a `UserRepository` typed as the interface, takes it through the constructor, and assigns it to a `final` field—whoever builds `UserService` supplies the concrete repository.
Now: (1) In tests, inject a mock. (2) In production, inject MySQLUserRepository. (3) Switch to PostgresUserRepository by changing one configuration — UserService doesn't change.

Spring automates this. You mark classes with `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Component`, and Spring creates them as beans, figures out what depends on what, and wires them together automatically. This whole system is called the **IoC Container** (Inversion of Control) — you give up control of object creation, and the container handles it.

- Constructor injection is preferred over field injection (@Autowired on a field) — it makes dependencies explicit, supports immutability (final fields), and works without Spring in tests
- IoC (Inversion of Control) is the principle; DI is the implementation technique. The Spring IoC Container creates and manages all beans.
- Three injection types: Constructor (preferred), Setter (@Autowired on setter), Field (@Autowired on field — avoid in production code)
- If there's only one constructor, Spring 4.3+ auto-injects without @Autowired annotation
- @Qualifier resolves ambiguity when multiple beans implement the same interface

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Spring Framework is a comprehensive Java framework for building enterprise applications — but it requires extensive XML or Java configuration for every feature.

Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of Spring that eliminates boilerplate: it auto-configures components, embeds a web server (Tomcat), and lets you start coding business logic immediately with minimal setup.

Think of Spring as a fully customizable toolkit, and Spring Boot as a pre-assembled workstation.

Saying Spring Boot replaces Spring — it doesn't. It uses Spring under the hood and just reduces configuration pain.
